title: Inter prepare new Jones bid at €35m for Liverpool after Akinsanmiro sale
description: After selling Ebeneezer Akinsanmiro to Monza, Inter are revitalising their pursuit of Liverpool midfielder Curtis Jones with fresh talks and an improved €35m offer ready.The Nerazzurri are looking t...
fullText:
After selling Ebeneezer Akinsanmiro to Monza, Inter are revitalising their pursuit of Liverpool midfielder Curtis Jones with fresh talks and an improved €35m offer ready.

The Nerazzurri are looking to the Premier League for reinforcements this summer after securing the Scudetto and Coppa Italia Double.

They already snapped up free agent John Stones from Manchester City, and are in advanced talks with Tottenham Hotspur for Cristian Romero at €40m.

LIVERPOOL, ENGLAND – APRIL 25: Curtis Jones of Liverpool during the Premier League match between Liverpool and Crystal Palace at Anfield on April 25, 2026 in Liverpool, England. (Photo by Alex Livesey/Getty Images)

Their next target is Jones, who will be a free agent at the end of the season, which is why Inter hope Liverpool will lower the €40m asking price.

Several previous proposals have been rejected, but multiple sources including the Corriere dello Sport, Tuttosport, Guardian and more maintain that a new and improved bid of €35m is on its way.

There were also rumours that Inter intermediaries were already in Liverpool over the last couple of days for negotiations.

PISA, ITALY – NOVEMBER 7: Ebenezer Akinsanmiro of Pisa Sporting Club in action during the Serie A match between Pisa SC and US Cremonese at Arena Garibaldi on November 7, 2025 in Pisa, Italy. (Photo by Gabriele Maltinti/Getty Images)

Meanwhile, the Nerazzurri need to make sales, and completed one today with midfielder Akinsanmiro sold to Monza.

That deal is believed to be worth €7.5m plus a 10 per cent cut of the future sale fee.

He spent last season on loan at Pisa.

title: Milan eye Brahim Diaz return as Leao future clouds Rossoneri summer
description: Milan are weighing a move to bring Brahim Díaz back to San Siro, as the Rossoneri search for a new attacking midfielder, with Rafael Leão’s uncertain future the dominant question over their summer...
fullText:
Milan are weighing a move to bring Brahim Díaz back to San Siro, as the Rossoneri search for a new attacking midfielder, with Rafael Leão’s uncertain future the dominant question over their summer.

According to CalcioMercato.com, citing the Corriere della Sera, Milan have identified Brahim as a candidate for the trequartista role having missed out on Greek teenager Konstantinos Karetsas, who joined Borussia Dortmund from Genk for €33m. Arsenal’s Ethan Nwaneri and Roma’s Matías Soulé are also under consideration.

A return for Brahim would reunite the Spanish-born Morocco international with a club he served well between 2020 and 2023, when he made 124 appearances on loan, scoring 18 goals and setting up 15 more while helping Milan to the 2022 Scudetto.

He remains under contract at Real Madrid until 2027, and Juventus had also been keen before pivoting to Bayer Leverkusen’s Kerim Alajbegović.

MAY 24: Rafael Leao of AC Milan looks on from the substitutes bench prior to the Serie A match between AC Milan and Cagliari Calcio at the Giuseppe Meazza Stadium on May 24, 2026 (Photo by Marco Luzzani/Getty Images)

The bigger call, however, concerns the man the Rossoneri may need to move on. Rafael Leão’s future remains the club’s principal talking point, with the Portugal forward having made clear he feels his seven-year spell is over.

His preference was for the Premier League or La Liga, but with no offers arriving from either, he has begun to open the door to Turkey.

There, Galatasaray are poised to make their move, and, unlike Fenerbahçe, are already assured of a place in the Champions League league phase.

Leão is receptive to the idea, though he is asking for a lucrative, double-digit salary to make the switch. Milan, for their part, would prefer a permanent sale, leaving the two sides, and the player’s wage demands, still some way apart.

title: 🐦 Richarlison the decider in Tottenham win over Chelsea in friendly
description: Even with one player less, Tottenham beat Chelsea 2-1 in a preseason friendly played this Saturday (1st) in Sydney, Australia.And it was thanks to Brazilian star Richarlison, who scored the winning go...
fullText:
Even with one player less, Tottenham beat Chelsea 2-1 in a preseason friendly played this Saturday (1st) in Sydney, Australia.

And it was thanks to Brazilian star Richarlison, who scored the winning goal deep into stoppage time.

The task became even harder when defender Danso was sent off in the second half, but “Pombo,” who started the match on the bench, stepped up and sealed the win for Roberto De Zerbi’s team.

Check out below the moment the striker found the back of the Blues’ net.

Before Richarlison’s decisive moment, the match had a lively first half.

Tonali put Spurs ahead, but Brazilian wonderkid Estêvão — making his first start after the injury that kept him out of the World Cup — leveled things for the Blues.

Chelsea also threatened through João Pedro in the second half, but he was denied by a great save from goalkeeper Kinsky, and in the end the night belonged to Tottenham’s No. 9.

The teams now enter the final stretch of preparation for the start of the 2026/27 Premier League season, which officially kicks off on August 21.

In the opening round, Tottenham visit Brentford on the 22nd, while Chelsea head to Fulham for their first official match of the season on the 24th.

title: Arsenal ownership approve anticipated figures to sign Real Madrid megastar Vinicius
description: According to The Athletic, The ownership group of Arsenal Football Club has officially given the green light to fund a blockbuster move for Real Madrid forward Vinicius Jr. The 26-year-old Brazilian i...
fullText:
According to The Athletic, The ownership group of Arsenal Football Club has officially given the green light to fund a blockbuster move for Real Madrid forward Vinicius Jr.

The 26-year-old Brazilian international has emerged as the Premier League club’s absolute top target to strengthen their attack, with the Gunners’ hierarchy prepared to commit massive financial resources to complete what would be one of the biggest transfers in football history.

Arsenal’s sporting department has been quietly working on this deal for months. Aware of the ongoing contract stalemate and growing lack of progress between Real Madrid and Vinicius, the Gunners have successfully positioned themselves to capitalise on the situation.

Sporting director Andrea Berta has already held preliminary talks with the player’s representatives.

Key figures at the North London club have conveyed a clear sporting message to the forward’s camp, promising that he would become the undisputed main star of a highly stable and ambitious Premier League project.

Arsenal prepared to go all-in on Vinicius. (Photo by Megan Briggs/Getty Images)

A move to Arsenal strongly appeals to Vinicius if he ultimately chooses not to sign an extension with Real Madrid.

Those within Arsenal believe that an agreement on personal terms will be straightforward should the player give his final approval.

“Mikel Arteta loves him,” a source with knowledge of the Arsenal manager’s outlook explained. “If he doesn’t renew, we will be there.”

To make the transfer possible, Arsenal’s owners have approved the daunting financial figures required for the total package. The Gunners are fully willing to break its traditional salary structure to accommodate Vinicius’ high wage demands.

Arteta wants Vinicius at Arsenal. (Photo by Michael Steele/Getty Images)

Arsenal also plan to use a substantial sign-on bonus and lucrative image rights agreements to bridge any financial gaps.

While the total expenditure is incredibly high, Arsenal’s board believes the costs will be quickly offset by a massive commercial windfall, as Vinicius is a global marketing powerhouse who could elevate the club’s brand to new heights.

The timing of Arsenal’s push relies heavily on Real Madrid’s growing contractual vulnerability. Vinicius has entered the final 12 months of his contract, which expires in June 2027.

Some officials within the Spanish club heavily fear a scenario where they lose one of their brightest stars for absolutely nothing next summer.

Furthermore, Real Madrid would be forced to pay the winger a significant loyalty bonus if he stays for the upcoming season without renewing.

Arsenal hope to take advantage of these factors to negotiate a significantly reduced transfer fee with Real Madrid, aiming to secure the winger before other European giants enter the race

title: Chelsea set to agree £26m deal for Chalobah to join Como
description: Chelsea are set to agree a deal for centre-back Trevoh Chalobah to join Como, Di Marzio reports.The Blues are closer than ever to reaching an agreement over the sale of their academy graduate, with ne...
fullText:
Chelsea are set to agree a deal for centre-back Trevoh Chalobah to join Como, Di Marzio reports.

The Blues are closer than ever to reaching an agreement over the sale of their academy graduate, with negotiations gathering pace over the past few days.

Chelsea have received an improved proposal from their Italian counterparts worth €28 million (£24m) plus performance-related bonuses.

The Italian club is also expected to submit another offer valued at €30m (£26m) plus bonuses, which could finally meet Chelsea’s expectations.

While the two clubs continue to work on the final details, the Chelsea centre-back has reportedly agreed personal terms with Como.

Chalobah is open to the move and is excited by the opportunity to continue his career in Italy. Chelsea have so far rejected two bids from Como, holding firm on their valuation of the defender.

The Blues were initially demanding a fee of around £35m but are ready to compromise.

With negotiations set to continue over the weekend, there is increasing confidence that the transfer could be completed in the coming days.

Como aren’t the only club interested in Chalobah. Inter Milan have admired the defender for some time, while another unnamed club has also been monitoring his situation.

However, Como are leading the race and one step away from finalising a deal.

The move would mark the end of Chalobah’s journey at Chelsea, where he progressed through the club’s famous academy before making his senior debut in 2021.

Since then, he has established himself as a reliable member of the first-team squad, making over 150 appearances for the Blues across all competitions.

A loan spell at Crystal Palace during the first half of the 2024/25 season helped revive his career before he returned to Stamford Bridge and had his busiest campaign at Chelsea.

Chalobah featured 47 times in all competitions last season and scored three goals. He was also part of Thomas Tuchel’s England squad at the World Cup.

title: Kelsey Mitchell makes double WNBA history in Fever’s win over Fire
description: Kelsey Mitchell passed Tina Thompson on the WNBA’s career 3-point list and tied Diana Taurasi with her 13th consecutive 20-point game.
fullText:
Kelsey Mitchell makes double WNBA history in Fever’s win over Fire originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

Kelsey Mitchell is not slowing down as the Indiana Fever continue their push toward the WNBA playoffs. Mitchell delivered another brilliant offensive performance Friday night, scoring 26 points in Indiana’s 112-98 victory over the Portland Fire. She shot 9-of-21 from the field and made four 3-pointers, helping the Fever pull away with a dominant second half.

Her latest scoring outburst also placed her in the WNBA record book in two different ways.

Mitchell surpassed Tina Thompson for sixth place on the league’s all-time list for made 3-pointers. She also recorded her 13th consecutive game with at least 20 points, tying Diana Taurasi for the second-longest streak in WNBA history. Only A’ja Wilson has produced a longer run. The Las Vegas Aces superstar scored at least 20 points in 20 consecutive games during the 2023 season.

Mitchell entered Friday with 747 career 3-pointers, leaving her two away from passing Thompson’s total of 748. She wasted little time taking care of that milestone.

The six-time All-Star knocked down four shots from beyond the arc, increasing her career total to 751. Mitchell now trails only Kayla McBride, Diana Taurasi, Sue Bird, Arike Ogunbowale and Sabrina Ionescu on the WNBA’s career list. Passing McBride for fifth place could take some time because the Minnesota Lynx veteran remains active and continues adding to her own total.

Mitchell’s ascension remains remarkable for a player who has spent her entire WNBA career with Indiana. The Fever selected her with the No. 2 overall pick in the 2018 draft, and she has steadily developed into one of the most dangerous perimeter scorers in league history.

Friday’s performance was another example of Mitchell’s ability to take control when Indiana needed an offensive spark.

She scored 11 points during the third quarter as the Fever turned a competitive game into a comfortable advantage. Indiana entered the fourth quarter leading by 18 and protected that cushion to secure the victory.

MORE: Kiki Iriafen, Cotie McMahon face WNBA fines after chippy Mystics-Wings game

Mitchell’s 3-point milestone was only half of her historic night. The 30-year-old has now scored at least 20 points in 13 consecutive games, matching one of the longest streaks ever produced by Taurasi.

Mitchell will have an opportunity to move ahead of Taurasi when Indiana faces the Lynx next. Reaching Wilson’s record would require seven more consecutive 20-point performances, but Mitchell’s current form makes that pursuit worth watching.

The next challenge will not be easy.

Minnesota owns one of the WNBA’s best defenses and will make limiting Mitchell a priority. Still, opposing teams have struggled to find an answer for the Fever star throughout her remarkable run. Mitchell has scored in a variety of ways, using her quick first step to attack the basket while remaining one of the league’s most dangerous long-range threats. Her scoring has helped Indiana emerge as one of the leading contenders in the Eastern Conference.

The Fever still have 15 regular-season games remaining, giving Mitchell plenty of time to climb additional lists and potentially challenge Wilson’s record. After making two pieces of WNBA history in the same night, Mitchell’s next performance has suddenly become even more compelling.

title: Mountaineer Nirmal Purja killed in Pakistan avalanche, his company says
description: The Nepali-born climber was known for scaling the world's 14 highest peaks in just over six months in 2019.
fullText:
Renowned mountaineer and former British Army soldier Nirmal Purja is among those killed in an avalanche on Broad Peak in Pakistan, his company has said.

Elite Expeditions shared the news on social media, saying it was with "profound sadness and immense heartbreak" that it confirmed Purja's death in Thursday's avalanche.

It also said that the other nine members of the expedition had died.

Purja, a Nepali-born climber, was known for scaling the world's 14 highest peaks in just over six months in 2019.

Pakistani officials previously said the bodies of three climbers - American Mallory Geis, Nadhira Ahmed Abdullah Al Harthy from Oman and Pur Bahadur Gurung from Nepal - who were among the 10-person expedition had been recovered.

Purja's death was also confirmed by Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah, who said on social media that "the tragic death of six Nepalese and four other foreign climbers, including world record holder Nirmal Purja, in the Karakoram mountain range of Pakistan, has shocked us".

"The history of their courage, dedication, and contributions will always remain inspiring," the prime minister added.

Rescue teams in Pakistan had been searching for the climbers on the world's 12th-highest summit.

Purjam 43, became widely known following a Netflix documentary chronicling his journey, 14 Peaks: Nothing Is Impossible, released in 2021.

The avalanche happened on Thursday on the 8,047m (26,400ft) peak in the Karakoram range.

The multinational climbing group was being led by Purja, who joined the British Army in 2003 and the Special Boat Service - the Royal Navy's special forces unit - in 2009.

Broad Peak is regarded as one of the more challenging mountains for climbers. The first successful ascent was in 1957, when an Austrian expedition reached the summit.

Since then, many more have climbed the mountain, but dozens have lost their lives.

One of Broad Peak's deadliest years was 2013, when at least six fatalities were recorded.

title: Aliyah Boston faces WNBA fine after heated exchange with Serah Williams
description: Aliyah Boston is expected to receive a $500 fine after a heated confrontation with Portland Fire forward Serah Williams.
fullText:
Aliyah Boston faces WNBA fine after heated exchange with Serah Williams originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

Aliyah Boston filled the box score during another Indiana Fever victory Friday night, but one heated moment will cost the All-Star center. Boston received her second technical foul of the season after getting into a tense exchange with Portland Fire forward Serah Williams during Indiana’s 112-98 win.

The incident occurred with 4:42 remaining in the third quarter. Boston and Williams made contact while battling for position before the situation quickly escalated. Boston appeared to strike Williams, who responded by pushing the Fever star. The two players then stared each other down before teammates and officials stepped between them.

Both Boston and Williams were assessed technical fouls. Under WNBA rules, each of a player’s first three technical fouls results in a $500 fine. Boston is therefore expected to lose $500 for her role in the confrontation, although she remains far from the league’s automatic suspension threshold.

Boston’s frustration came during an otherwise quiet third quarter for the former No. 1 overall pick. She played more than seven minutes in the period but did not attempt a field goal or score a point. Her exchange with Williams added more tension to what had become an increasingly physical game.

Even more interesting was Serah Williams and Aliyah Boston getting into it.

🎥 @sluggahjells#WNBAhttps://t.co/8E2mPqx99Mpic.twitter.com/Op2qQJt2Nu

— The Whole Delivery (@TWDTV1) August 1, 2026

The confrontation did not develop into anything more serious. Teammates and officials separated the two players before the situation could escalate, and both remained in the game. Boston has largely avoided disciplinary issues during her WNBA career.

Her only previous technical foul this season came during a June matchup against the New York Liberty. Friday’s whistle increased her total to two, leaving her six away from an automatic one-game suspension.

Players are fined $500 for each of their first three technical fouls. The penalty increases to $1,000 for technicals Nos. 4 through 7. An eighth technical brings a $1,500 fine and a one-game suspension.

With only 15 regular-season games remaining, Boston would need an unlikely run of technical fouls to reach that limit.

MORE: Kelsey Mitchell makes double WNBA history in Fever’s win over Fire

The technical foul should not overshadow everything Boston contributed against Portland. She finished with 14 points, nine rebounds, six assists, five steals and two blocks, nearly producing a double-double while impacting nearly every area of the game.

Boston’s five steals matched a season high and helped Indiana create additional scoring opportunities in transition. Her six assists also reflected her development as a facilitator within the Fever’s talented offense. Kelsey Mitchell led Indiana with 26 points, extending her streak of games with at least 20 points to 13. The Fever scored 112 points and built an 18-point advantage entering the fourth quarter before completing another convincing victory.

Indiana improved to 19-10 and moved into fourth place in the overall WNBA standings. The Fever have emerged as one of the league’s hottest teams as the playoff race begins to intensify. Boston remains essential to that pursuit because of her scoring, rebounding, defense and ability to create opportunities for teammates.

Friday’s confrontation will make her $500 lighter, but it did little to diminish an impressive all-around performance in another important Fever victory.

title: England's Maguire wins gold in T54 1500m
description: England's Nathan Maguire wins the T54 1500m at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow to retain the title he won four years ago in Birmingham.
fullText:
England's Nathan Maguire won the T54 1500m at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow to retain the title he won four years ago in Birmingham.

The 28-year-old Paralympic silver medallist found space on the inside of the track and pushed hard to break away from the field, finishing in a time of three minutes 17.65 seconds.

England team-mate Daniel Sidbury took silver behind him, just as he did in 2022.

The gold medal is England's fifth in athletics at the Games so far, following victories for Georgia Hunter Bell, Thomas Young, Sophie Hahn and Zac Shaw.

Later on Saturday, Hahn took silver in the T38 200m, beaten by Australian gold medallist Rhiannon Clarke.

title: Bayern Munich News: No more pressure for player sales at FC Bayern; Details on the plan for a striker in 2027; and MORE!
description: FC Bayern might not make any more moves this summer.
fullText:
Is Uli Hoeneß mellowing in his old age? Say it ain’t so! After months of pushing for sales, the Bayern Munich legend is relieving board member for sport Max Eberl of that pressure. While Hoeneß wants to see a few sales, it is no longer a requirement for Eberl to keep his job.

“If we can now manage to move one or two players on — which is what we’d ideally like to do — that would be great. But I also want to make one thing absolutely clear: a contract with Bayern Munich is sacrosanct. That means if, in the end, no suitable solution is found, we’ll keep the players,” Hoeneß said.

This is pretty significant as Bayern Munich has three pretty expensive surplus players on the roster at the moment. Per Capology, João Palhinha (€12,000,000 total pay package), Bryan Zaragoza (€8,490,000 total pay package), and Sacha Boey (€4,340,000 total pay package) all carry significant financial burdens without much hope for playing time.

Another big candidate for sale is Hiroki Itō (€4,700,000 total pay package), but as the squad’s fourth center-back, he — at least — has a role that would be needed and a pay package commensurate with his role.

No doubt, Eberl will still try to unload those aforementioned players (and maybe a few youngsters as well), but not feeling like he will lose his job if he cannot move those players is like a big relief.

Manchester United seems to have its eyes on a few Real Madrid players, including midfielder Eduardo Camavinga:

Manchester United are exploring a move for Real Madrid midfielder Eduardo Camavinga. Nicolo Schira reports that Los Blancos are now willing to listen to offers to sign the 23-year-old, who was previously viewed as a key player for the club’s future project. Camavinga is one of several players to have been linked with a switch to Old Trafford, where it looks as though the club’s hierarchy are plotting one more marquee addition in midfield after recently confirming the signings of Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans.

Earlier this week, we saw the report break about Bayern Munich potentially looking to add a striker in the summer of 2027. Now, Sport Bild journalist Christian Falk wants to expand on the information a bit:

✅ It is TRUE: There is an idea to give Harry Kane a deeper role as he gets older at Bayern Munich. The striker knows he’s not getting faster as the years progress, but everyone can see that he already has an important role at FC Bayern with his passing and playmaking ability. So, he already has in his mind that he could play deeper and leave room for a pure striker ahead of him. This idea was already developing at the club when Vincent Kompany first joined in 2024, which was why Bayern had the idea to bring Benjamin Šeško to Munich. He was too expensive at the time, which is why Manchester United ended up pulling off the deal a year later.

However, the idea is still there to bring such a striker into the team. Now, Bayern have Ismael Saibari who can cover this role as well. So Bayern will perhaps see if they can make it work already this coming season. So they have to see if they’ll still need a player like Šeško down the line. The Slovenian is still on the list and he’s a player who’s very interesting for FC Bayern. Perhaps, if he’s struggling to make his mark in the Premier League, they could return to this idea. The plan for the future, nonetheless, is to sign another striker who can be a Harry Kane successor but also play in a two-striker system. This is one of Vincent Kompany’s key ideas.

On the surface, it does make sense, but there are a lot of variables, including what the new contracts look like for other attackers like Harry Kane and Michael Olise; along with how players like Saibari, Lennart Karl, and Arijon Ibrahimović perform over the course of this season.

Juventus is still reportedly toying with the idea of bringing in Joshua Zirkzee:

Juventus are discussing a move for Manchester United striker Joshua Zirkzee, The Sun reports. Both clubs are said to be in advanced talks regarding an initial loan deal that would include an option to be made permanent for £30 million, with the 25-year-old identified by Juve i as an alternative to Paris Saint-Germain forward Randal Kolo Muani. Zirkzee scored just two goals in 24 Premier League appearances last season.

ESPN would later come back with additional information as well:

Juventus have registered their interest in Manchester United forward Joshua Zirkzee, sources have told ESPN. United are open to offers for the Netherlands international and would prefer a straight transfer. Juventus are exploring all options including a season-long loan with an obligation or option to make the move permanent.

Paris Saint-Germain is out on a pursuit of Manchester City star midfielder Rodri:

Paris Saint-Germain have no interest in Manchester City midfielder Rodri, who has recently been linked with Real Madrid.

However, Real Madrid could actually be getting close to a deal with the City star per ESPN:

Real Madrid are confident of reaching an agreement to sign Manchester City midfielder Rodri after holding positive talks with the Spain international, according to AS. Personal terms are understood to be in place, with the LaLiga side now focused on agreeing a transfer fee with City, who have already rejected an initial approach. Madrid remain optimistic a deal can be completed, as Rodri is keen on returning to Spain after entering the final year of his contract at the Etihad Stadium.

Former Borussia Dortmund and Bayer Leverkusen midfielder Julian Brandt has made the move to Ajax:

Julian Brandt, Ajacied. pic.twitter.com/dGbCthctL6

— AFC Ajax (@AFCAjax) July 31, 2026

Marc-André ter Stegen is also rumored to be on the way to Ajax as well per Diario Sport:

🔵🔴 Marc André Ter Stegen en el aeropuerto de Birmingham se marcha a Amsterdam

🚨 Deja la concentración del Barça

📹 @ferrancorreas pic.twitter.com/4zH5BUNjk6

— Diario SPORT (@sport) July 31, 2026

Bayern Munich is reportedly not feeling great about being able to sell João Palhinha to Aston Villa:

Bayern are not particularly confident, at the moment, that a deal will be struck with Aston Villa for João Palhinha. They’ve tried to put pressure on the player, but the Portuguese international has also put the pressure back on the club by insisting that he’s going to stay put if Bayern are determined to attach a high asking price to him and there aren’t any clubs available that he’d like to join. This is hard for Bayern, as they do want to sell him.

There is still a big hope that Aston Villa will come in with an offer. I think he’d fit in perfectly at this great club. I saw the midfielder in training on Wednesday, and I have to say that he’s doing really well. The players were giving him a hard time but he gave as good as he got! He almost picked up an injury, such was the intensity of his showing. He wanted to show that he’s good enough for Bayern and, of course, good enough for a big club like Villa. I think we should keep an eye on him. But, at the moment, it’s all a bit quiet.

Chelsea attacker Mykhailo Mudryk is cleared from his ban and will return to the club. What lies ahead, though, is very cloudy for the now 25-year-old:

🚨🔵 OFFICIAL: Mykhailo Mudryk is clear to play again after doping accusations. Case settled.

Mudryk, expected to join Chelsea in Hong Kong for pre-season tour. He’s gonna be available immediately. pic.twitter.com/VCk6c74NVU

— Fabrizio Romano (@FabrizioRomano) July 31, 2026

At one point, Mudryk was on Bayern Munich’s radar. While a move is not happening, could this be a potential value buy next summer? Would it even make sense?

Right now, the full focus will be on Chelsea figuring out if Mudryk can still play at a high level.

Romano later checked in with a statement from Chelsea:

🔵🇺🇦 Mykhaylo Mudryk travels on Sunday to Hong Kong to re-join Chelsea with immediate effect.

“We know how much this opportunity to return means to him. Our focus now is on supporting Misha’s reintegration into the squad and helping him resume his career. Everyone at the Club now looks forward to helping Misha return to full fitness, back into the squad and back onto the pitch”.

title: Jim Dandy 2026: Renegade’s And Commandment’s Battle With Chip Honcho
description: True is, every horse in today's talent-rich Jim Dandy is going to get to the line in a different way. Here's how those differences stack up among the favorites.
fullText:
Race days – and specifically this lovely Jim Dandy race day at Saratoga – have a way of debunking much of the fluff as we all drill down to what we’re going to lay on the barrelhead, backing whom. The windows beckon at the Spa. The money has yet to speak, but it will.

But before we dive into what Commandment may do to Renegade, or vice versa, or how Chip Honcho could just possibly squeak by to whip them both, we’ll tip the hat to the origins of today’s race and the venerable reputation of Saratoga’s (alleged) track bias favoring speed, or at least its “graveyard of champions” legend that (supposedly) favors upsets of a grand order.

First and foremost, the morning refresher on the field and the morning line:

1. Chip Honcho, Steve Asmussen, Jose Ortiz, 3-1

2. Asked and Answered, Antonio Arriaga, Jaime Rodriguez, 30-1

3. Renegade, Todd Pletcher, Irad Ortiz Jr., 7-5

4. Silent Tactic, Mark Casse, Luis Saez, 6-1

5. Commandment, Brad Cox, Flavien Prat, 6-5

The story is this: In 1964, the Saratoga grandees decided to inaugurate this afternoon’s race, a Travers prep, by insouciantly naming it for the 100-1 longshot Jim Dandy, who, at Saratoga in 1930, infamously toppled that year’s Triple Crown victor Gallant Fox in the mud. Going off at 1-2, Gallant Fox had been considered a dead-sure thing.

Fast forward to June 2026: Two months ago on this reputed spoiler of a track, nothing was “spoiled” by anything like a “speed bias.” Rather, in the 158th Belmont running, three Triple Crown deep closers famously battled it out down the lane, speed nowhere in sight.

Kentucky Derby winner Golden Tempo certified his victorious Churchill Downs close with yet another breathtakingly dominant close that simply shut down the game Commandment, who just had no tools and no ability to match the immense power of of the winner’s last-furlong surge. After a really rough Belmont trip, Renegade held on to show.

This article was originally published on Forbes.com

fullText:
New AI models, advanced robots and specialty computer chips are unsettling markets and the US tech industry

Over the past month, a series of advancements in China’s artificial intelligence, chip manufacturing and robotics technologies have rattled financial markets, caused divisions among US tech moguls and left the Trump administration scrambling to respond.

Silicon Valley has long pointed to China’s tech industry as a competitive threat and used its growth as rationale for why US firms should not face regulatory oversight that could slow them down. In recent weeks, however, China’s progress has pushed US tech CEOs past vague warnings and into open disagreement over how to address Chinese-made products upending their industry.

The most immediate threat to Silicon Valley’s status quo has come from a series of Chinese-made open-source, open-weight AI models that are free to download and use. The models, such as Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3, are powerful enough to compete in some applications with proprietary and comparatively expensive AI products from OpenAI and Anthropic.

The emergence of China’s open-source AI alternatives has caused divisions in both the White House and US tech industry over whether to oppose or embrace these new models. On one side are chip manufacturers who see revenue opportunities from increased AI usage and tech companies concerned about OpenAI and Anthropic’s growing dominance in the AI industry. On the other is Anthropic and OpenAI, which face profit pressures from open source models and argue that Chinese-made models pose security risks.

The White House is similarly divided, historically hawkish on China’s tech industry but wary of blocking low-cost AI models that American businesses have come to rely on. Treasury secretary Scott Bessent suggested in recent weeks that the US could sanction Chinese AI firms over alleged intellectual property theft from American companies, while commerce secretary Howard Lutnick has received letters from tech-startup founders asking him not to cut off access to open models.

Amid reports that the Trump administration was considering banning or limiting the use of China’s open source models, a swath of prominent big tech companies including Microsoft, Nvidia, Palantir and Meta also recently published a letter urging lawmakers to refrain from putting restrictions on open models. Additionally, Nvidia’s CEO Jensen Huang went to Capitol Hill on Tuesday to meet with Democratic and Republican party leaders to lobby in support of open models.

While facing heat from China and other tech companies, OpenAI and Anthropic revealed in recent weeks that their AI models went rogue during cybersecurity tests and hacked into outside organizations. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman visited lawmakers and administration officials this week to discuss controls on AI following the incident. That forced Donald Trump to field questions about whether he would put more safety restrictions on AI development.

“We have to be careful in both ways. We don’t want to restrict them when all of a sudden we come in second to China,” Trump said, adding: “I know many of these people. I don’t want to restrict them from doing great work.”

While the Trump administration debates potential safety controls and limits on Chinese-made AI models, it took tangible action this week against China’s increasingly prominent robotics industry. The Federal Communications Commission announced on Tuesday a ban on humanoid robots from China over what it alleged was an unacceptable national security risk.

China’s humanoid robots from companies such as Unitree have been the subject of numerous viral videos this year, showcasing their ability to dance or interact with people when programmed to do so. The FCC alleged that the robots could also steal data or surveil US citizens, as well as threaten US manufacturing and supply chains.

The FCC’s decision further escalates the US competition with China over emerging technologies and comes as fears over China’s tech have shifted financial markets. A report from the Information this week stating that China had begun mass production of specialty chips key to the AI boom spurred a stock selloff that erased $1tn in market value from other chip manufacturers.

As Chinese-made tech advancements increasingly begin to rival their US counterparts, Silicon Valley’s divisions could intensify, markets could become more skittish and the Trump administration could face more pressure over how to counter China’s influence.

title: The great British switch-off: how floating retreats, mobile-free pubs and sauna book groups are freeing people from their smartphones

fullText:
Sick of doomscrolling? From venues with smartphone swear jars to cabins with absolutely no signal, here are the fun and freeing ways to ditch your device

There’s a ritual at the start of every event hosted by the Offline Project. Run by Pelé Zachariah, the activities vary – it could be a group walk, a collage‑making class or a supper club – but each one begins in the same way, *with an invitation to hand over your phone. Devices go in a lockbox. Once they’re all in, Zachariah closes the door and turns the key. “I don’t place them in for people, because it’s nice for them to physically put it in the box themselves, walk away, and think: for the next two or three hours, I’m fully present.”

He has been running these screen-free events in London since August 2025. First-timers can be apprehensive about being separated from their phone. “You can sense the vibe when they’re putting it away,” says Zachariah. “People have said to me, ‘I felt really weird’ or ‘I felt super uncomfortable for the first few minutes not having my phone on me.’ Then they’ll say, ‘I didn’t know how much I needed that.’”

Zachariah understands why people might find it difficult at first. “It’s very unnatural. You might put your phone in the living room while you work in the kitchen, but here you’re seeing it locked behind what is essentially a gate that you can’t access,” he says. But when people leave, they often say they would like to have their own phone lockbox, or tell him that they’re going to try to not look at their device until they get home. “It’s kind of sad that we have to literally lock our phones away. But people really crave that time.”

This is true for Jarred Laros, 31, who lives in Essex and has been a regular at the Offline Project since it launched. One of the first events he went to was a “paint and sip” evening, where an artist taught everyone how to paint a landscape scene with mountains, a river and a sunset. People sat around a table together, working on their canvases while having drinks and snacks, and getting to know each other. “I liked the idea of getting off my phone and being more intentional with how I’m spending my time. I would never try to teach myself how to paint, but doing that in a community setting is very easy-going. The conversation flows.”

Laros runs his own business, and spends a lot of time on his devices. “I’m always glued to a screen, whether it’s my iPad, my MacBook, my phone, or all three at the same time,” he says. “Outside of work, there’s the doomscroll that you succumb to. I go on Instagram without intending to. Half an hour later, I’m, like, ‘What am I still doing on this app?’ My average daily screen time is seven and a half hours. My relationship with my phone is not what I want it to be.”

The Offline Project is part of a new wave of digital detox communities that host events to give people time away from screens. It’s not hard to understand the appeal: adults in the UK now spend an average of four and a half hours online a day, and most of that is on their phones, according to Ofcom’s 2025 Online Nation report.

In 2025, the annual TouchPoints survey by the Institute of Practitioners in Advertising found that British adults were spending more time on their phones than watching TV for the first time. The government has recently announced that in spring 2027 it will bring in a social media ban for under-16s, which will include platforms like Instagram, TikTok and YouTube. When the news was announced, a teenage girl went viral when asked by a news reporter how she would spend all her newfound free time. Her answer? “Stare at a wall.”

Thankfully, if you want a break from your phone, there are plenty of things to do that are much more engaging. As our lives are becoming ever-more online, people are starting to push back against the hold that technology has on us. Sick of looking out at a sea of screens, some musicians are enforcing a no phones policy at their gigs. Bob Dylan’s 2025 UK and Ireland tour, Fred Again’s gigs at Alexandra Palace in February, and Harry Styles’s one-off gig in Manchester in March this year all had rules against using phones. It’s happening at comedy events, too – phones were placed in locked pouches at Sarah Silverman’s London Palladium gig last year, and Russell Howard’s current Don’t Tell the Algorithm tour promises “no phones, no distractions, just humans and jokes”.

According to data from Eventbrite, attendance at phone-free events in 2024 to 2025 increased by 121% globally. At broadcaster and DJ Annie Mac’s club night Before Midnight, stickers are placed on phone cameras so you can’t take photos or videos. “It reminds people to be in the moment. You’re only going to get so much satisfaction out of blurred videos with distorted sound, or dark, fuzzy photos,” she says. “Nightclubs are traditionally places where you go to feel a sense of freedom – to be whoever you want to be. They’re meant to be dark for that dual sense of losing yourself and finding yourself at the same time. Phones inhibit both of those things.”

While some are seeking out pockets of time at events and venues where they can escape their smartphones, others are going one step further and ditching them altogether. Cody Ramone, 31, from Derby, was using an old flip phone from 2015 until the pandemic, when life became more online than ever and he needed a smartphone again. In 2024, he switched back to a “dumb phone”. “I got tired of all the notifications and being constantly online,” he says.

Abandoning his smartphone has been transformative and given him time for more enriching activities. “I get bored more. Being bored is what drives you to try new things, pick up an old hobby, or think creatively. My attention span has improved, so I read more and spend more time doing creative hobbies, like crochet. I call people or hang out with them more often,” he says.

What is it that makes our phones so addictive? “Digital media activates the same reward pathway as drugs and alcohol, releasing dopamine, our reward neurotransmitter, in a key area of the reward pathway in the brain,” says Anna Lembke, professor of psychiatry at Stanford University School of Medicine and the author of Dopamine Nation. “Moving images are like catnip for the mammalian brain, leading to video-chaining, akin to ‘chain smoking’. Once we begin, it’s hard to stop, even when we want to.”

The more time we spend on our phones, the more we become “desensitised to what we are seeing” and look for more “potent rewards to recreate that original experience of pleasure”, says Lembke. “At the same time, we lose our ability to take joy in other more modest rewards, like watching a sunset, sharing a meal with friends, or reading a good book. We spend more time scrolling alone. We become increasingly dissatisfied and lonely.”

While that might sound like a bleak state of affairs, the good news is that it doesn’t have to be this way. With the rise of phone-free experiences, it’s possible to detach yourself from your device, even if it’s temporarily. “Part of having a healthier relationship with technology must include discrete periods of time when we are not using it, and instead fully present and interacting with the people and the world around us,” says Lembke. “This means creating collective spaces where we come together device-free.”

From off-grid, tech-free cabins to the pubs where devices aren’t allowed, these are the places to escape your phone in the UK.

Set up in Amsterdam in 2024 by friends Jordy van Bennekom, Valentijn Klok and Ilya Kneppelhout, the Offline Club has 14 chapters in cities across 10 countries, including London and Bristol in the UK. Events start with everyone putting their devices in the “phone hotel”, a lockable metal box with slots. For the first hour, there’s music playing but no talking, and everyone does their own thing. For the second hour, people are encouraged to chat.

The demand for these kinds of events is growing. In London there’s the Switch Off – quiet, phone-free sessions for women where they can journal, collage or read a book – while the Offline Project hosts screen-free walks, talks and workshops. Logging Off Club is a UK initiative – with local groups in London, Bristol, Brighton, Southampton, Cambridge and the New Forest – that has now expanded to Sydney, Mexico City and Winnipeg.

In Bath, friends Nicola MacDonald and Laura Hughes started the Digital Detox Club in early 2025. They host events every two months at The Den cafe in Bath – phones go into the “tech motel” on arrival, and the pair provide optional activities like board games, journalling and crafts. “We’ve been struck by the diversity of attendees, from university students to retirees, which suggests this isn’t a niche concern,” says MacDonald. “It reflects a broader cultural fatigue with constant connectivity.”

If you’re trying to spend less time on your phone, a craft class does some of the work for you by keeping your hands busy. But there are specifically phone‑free classes, too. Native Hands offers basketry, pottery and bushcraft sessions, held outside in an ancient woodland in Sussex. At Curious House in East Sussex, classes range from basket weaving to portrait painting. All sessions start with a mindful breathing exercise to help people switch off.

In November last year, Dan Palmer launched Airplane Mode – a monthly phone-free event at his organic restaurant and natural wine bar, Eat Your Greens, in Leeds. The free events include workshops hosted by local creatives, doing things like painting, collage and origami.

Rather than locking phones away in a safe, they use a swear jar system. “Every time I catch anyone on their phone, I fine them 50p,” Palmer says. “All the fines go to a charity called Positive Action for Refugees and Asylum Seekers. So far, I’ve issued three fines – and one of them was for me! No one wants to be on their phones when they have something more interesting to do.”

The idea of using your hands to make something tangible rather than doomscrolling is what inspired Nadia Butt from Inner Canvas to host art sessions for women at her home in Reading without the distraction of screens. “The screen-free element is at the heart of the sessions,” she says. “We treat it like a ritual. At the start of each session, phones are silenced and placed in a box. I call it the ‘phone spa’. Framing it as something collective removes the anxiety around it.”

Spas are all about relaxing and switching off, but often these spaces aren’t phone-free. That is changing, though, with some spas now enforcing phone bans. The Bath Thermae Spa has a strict no phones policy – guests must put devices in a lockable pouch that’s kept in their locker. At Careys Manor in the New Forest, there’s a digital detox spa break, which includes relaxing treatments, a complimentary journal and a phone amnesty box in the room.

Phones have been banned at the Bothy at Heckfield Place, Hampshire, since it launched in 2023. “Seeing someone on their phone in a space dedicated to restoration felt out of alignment. You are there to be with yourself, to listen inwardly, to slow down,” says the spa operations director, Reka Seres-Erdei.

It’s not just at spas – as sauna culture rapidly grows, many people are finding these spaces offer a welcome break from technology. Ryan Haynes, 34, is a regular at London’s Community Sauna Baths, which has locations in Camberwell, Hackney Wick, Stratford, Walthamstow and Peckham. You can’t take your phone into the sauna, but you’re allowed to take photos outside, although they are considering a phone ban throughout.

Haynes’s Wednesday morning sauna session is “non-negotiable” for him. “All of my best ideas in the past two years have been while sitting in a sauna. Everyone needs to slow down to hear what’s going on in their brain,” he says.

As an independent bookshop owner and a sauna enthusiast, Kelly Wickson had an inspired idea last year: a book club in a sauna. Wickson owns Chapter 34 in Shoreham-by-Sea on the Sussex coast, and hosts the sauna book club once a month at the Nomadic Sauna on Kingston Beach. Creating a phone-free space was a big part of it, and the sauna conveniently ticks that box. “It will ruin your phone; you’ve got no choice,” she says.

The books are always 250 pages or less, and there’s no commitment to go every month. Phones are left in waterproof tubs outside the sauna. The book club is an hour long, and they go in and out of the sauna throughout, with some having a quick dip in the sea during breaks. Wickson has been amazed at how popular it is. “We do it on a Friday evening and it sells out,” she says.

While a book club in a sauna is particularly unusual, people increasingly value being given the time and space to switch off and read. This is the thinking behind Silent Book Club, where one of the mottoes is: “Put down your phone, pick up a book.” It’s a global network with about 2,000 chapters in more than 60 countries, and there are almost 150 in the UK and Ireland.

When Camille Jetzer and James Nasmyth opened the Roses of Elagabalus in Dalston, east London, last year, they knew they wanted to minimise phone use. They refer to it as a “clubhouse” – there’s a bar, restaurant, dancing and cabaret. “The idea of having no phones is that you would walk into the Roses, leave the outside world behind and enter this fantasy world where you can just enjoy the moment,” Jetzer says.

When you arrive at the Roses, a host explains that there’s no photography, and places a sticker over your phone camera. There are also reminders on the menus. “It’s a ‘you were there or you missed it’ situation,” Jetzer says, who has also noticed their regular punters reminding new visitors about the rule.

While phones aren’t locked away, Jetzer says the stickers on cameras mean they are used less. “It creates an environment where phones are less desired. In a dream world, we’d lock away the phones. That’s maybe next year’s project,” she says.

Elsewhere in London, Esmeralda’s Mayfair and the Spy Bar at Raffles London at the OWO both put stickers on phone cameras. In 2019, Samuel Smith’s pubs brought in a rule that customers couldn’t use phones or laptops in their establishments, of which there are more than 200 across the country. At the Barrel at Bude in Cornwall, anyone who breaks its no phones rule has to donate £1, which goes to local charities. In Herne Bay in Kent, the Butchers Arms has been a phone-free zone since it opened in 2005 – there are no signs needed to enforce it, says owner Martyn Hillier. “A disgruntled look from other customers is enough. If that doesn’t work we all start saying, ‘Rhubarb, rhubarb, rhubarb’, louder and louder until they realise they can’t converse any more.”

In Woking, Kim and Mike Jarred run Beyond the Screen, a monthly phone-free social at their local pub the Olive Tree. They set it up in March 2025 after talking about how they could model good phone habits for their teenage sons. They provide activities like puzzles and conversation starters, but mostly people just sit and chat. “Pubs are closing down and we’re just staying in our houses with our phones in front of our faces rather than getting out and meeting people. We’re human beings, and we need to connect with each other. Phones are getting in the way of that,” Kim says.

“Nights out now can feel like content creation exercises. We wanted to remove that layer entirely and return the focus to the room,” says James Hutchins, co-founder of Manchester club Amber’s. It opened in December 2024 and has a no-photo, no‑video policy, with stickers placed over phone cameras. “If people are seen taking photos or videos inside the club, they are politely asked to leave,” Hutchins says.

Amber’s is part of a growing trend in UK clubs, as more venues are making their dancefloors a phone‑free space. The policy is used at both Fold and Fabric in London, Lakota and sister venue Moon Club in Bristol, and Doppler Studio in Leicester. Some clubs ban phones completely. At Offgrid, a monthly day party at House Party in Soho, London, co‑founded by Stormzy, phones are sealed in a locked pouch. At her club night Before Midnight, Annie Mac has noticed a palpable shift in atmosphere – something she experienced during the first phone‑free Before Midnight event at the Warehouse Project in Manchester. “People were more present and louder. They whooped, they hollered, they whistled. They reacted to the tunes in a visceral way.”

In 2019, Hector Hughes was working for a tech startup in London and feeling burnt out. “I ended up at a silent retreat at a Buddhist temple on top of a mountain in the Himalayas. When you got there, they took your phone off you. I spent 10 days cut off from the outside world. It was a revelation,” says Hughes.

He came back from that trip, quit his job and started setting up Unplugged – off-grid cabins in the UK where you lock your phone away. It launched in the summer of 2020; there are now 60 digital detox cabins around the country (and they have expanded to Catalonia, too). The phone-free element is self‑policed, but each cabin has a lock box with a padlock, and the key is in a sealed envelope. They provide a Polaroid camera, a map and an old-school Nokia phone in case of emergencies. Hughes says that Unplugged’s customers often return for regular stays and go on to make changes in their daily lives, like having phone-free date nights or drastically cutting down their screen time.

If you like the idea of escaping to an off-grid cabin and ditching your phone, there are various options around the UK. Unyoked’s cabins run on solar power, have no wifi and often no phone signal – there’s a “spice signal”, from mild to extra spicy, to set expectations for how remote a cabin feels, and how long it might take to walk to one. They also have Brick devices, which help you block certain apps from your phone for a set amount of time. Similarly, Shacks’ cabins are off-grid with no wifi, and lockboxes for phones.

Alternatively, you could look for a remote cottage with no wifi and limited or no phone signal, like the Cottage in the Clouds in the middle of the Lake District national park, or Woodcock Cabin in the Cambrian mountains in Wales. If you want to escape dry land, too, Lilypod in Devon is a floating retreat with three solar-powered eco pods built on a platform next to a lake, where there’s no TV, wifi or phone signal, but there are board games, beanbags and a king-sized bed.

Florence Achery, founder of Yoga Retreats and More, launched her “Retreat like it’s 1999” digital detox breaks, in Lancashire and Cumbria, in 2023. A recent guest enjoyed the break from her devices so much that she forgot to pack her laptop and phone when she left. “I had to WhatsApp the guest she was travelling with to get them to pick up her stuff,” Achery says.

On arrival, guests hand over their devices before spending the next few days sharing meals together, going on long walks, doing yoga and star gazing. “They’re in charge, not their phones,” says Achery, who gives her guests a battery-powered alarm clock to take home, to encourage them to keep phones out of their bedrooms. She has also launched a parent and teen digital detox retreat to help younger people to change their relationship with technology.

At its 223-hectare (550-acre) estate on the River Dart in Devon, the Sharpham Trust hosts retreats focused on mindfulness and connecting to nature; guests are encouraged to switch off their phones.

And, in Suffolk, sisters Lauretta and Sharon Gavin host regular phone-free retreats at the Detox Barn, where guests enjoy vegan food, yoga, sound baths and countryside walks. “For many people it’s a huge relief to step away from their phones for 48 hours,” Lauretta says. “People open up, share stories and properly connect.”

fullText:
Agents withdraw Jerry Falade’s hotly anticipated debut after saying they can no longer authenticate ‘how the manuscript evolved’

A high-profile publishing deal for a debut crime novel has collapsed after doubts emerged over whether artificial intelligence played a role in writing it.

The hotly anticipated manuscript Call Me, I’ll Hide the Body, by Jerry Falade, was withdrawn from sale by its agent despite reportedly receiving an offer for more than $2m (£1.5m) from Minotaur, owned by Macmillan US, as part of a 14-way auction. The plan was to publish it in 2028.

An email sent to publishers by Falade’s agents and seen by the Guardian said: “Jerry Falade produced an incredible manuscript that dazzled us and the top publishing professionals around the world. Unfortunately, we are no longer able to authenticate how the manuscript fully evolved from origin to completion.”

It continued: “During the submission process we vetted the manuscript with Jerry for AI and felt trusting in his reassurance that it was written without utilising AI as a resource in the writing or editorial process. We can no longer substantiate that, and we are withdrawing the book.”

The US auction was run by the author’s agent Marc Gerald of Europa Content, according to the Bookseller. In the UK, Sandy Hodgman of Hodgman Literary is said to have secured several six-figure bids through a similarly competitive process. The Guardian has approached both agents for comment.

Gerald told the Bookseller he first read the book in June, and that it was “stunningly good, everyone fell in love with it. It’s a book that appeals to absolutely everyone.”

He said that halfway through the submissions process, an editor raised concerns that the book had signs of potential AI use. Gerald said Europa opted against using AI-detection software to check the manuscript, saying Falade was “clear and credible” in his explanation.

However, after a meeting on 29 July, when “aspects of [Falade’s] story changed”, the agency decided to cut ties, citing the “need to have total faith”.

“We feel terrible for putting this into the universe and the firestorm it has caused,” Gerald added. “The book itself is genius – however it came to be drafted, it’s amazing.”

Falade’s case is the latest in a string of controversies to hit publishing this year, as authors, agents and publishers grapple with how to handle suspected AI use in manuscripts. Earlier this year, Hachette pulled the US release of Mia Ballard’s horror novel Shy Girl after rumours circulated online that the author had relied on AI, something she denies.

In a statement to the Guardian, Falade rejected claims that he had used AI and said the response reflected racial bias in publishing.

He said: “Three Black authors received major publishing deals this year, and all three later had deals cancelled or disrupted following suspicions about AI. There seems to be a troubling assumption that when a Black writer produces work that attracts significant attention, the work could not possibly be their own. Meanwhile, there are popular white writers who have publicly mentioned using AI for their writing processes and they’re still doing fine.”

Falade did not name other authors, but two Black authors in the US – Ballard and HM Wolfe, author of the viral romance Daggermouth – faced allegations of AI use this year. Wolfe also denies she used AI.

Falade said: “In my case, rumours began circulating and, within six hours, I had been dropped by my agency, deals were paused, and press releases were being issued.” He added that AI-detection tools “are widely known to produce false positives”. He said the novel had “passed through first readers, second readers, editors, and acquisitions teams at numerous publishing houses … If the manuscript had shown genuine signs of being generated by AI, it is difficult to believe that every one of those experienced professionals would have failed to notice.”

title: Courting controversy and befriending Trump - the story of Fifa boss Infantino
description: Gianni Infantino has clashed with unions and European football, but after 10 years as Fifa president he remains in a powerful position.
fullText:
Gianni Infantino has been Fifa president for 10 years, when he was elected with a remit to rescue football's world governing body.

The decade since has been one of reform, expansion and, more recently, controversy.

Infantino was installed with Fifa engulfed by claims of widespread corruption and after predecessor Sepp Blatter had resigned.

Fifa's finances were in a desperate state. There was a reported $550m (£392m) black hole, external after sponsors walked away.

In Infantino, the game felt it had found a safe pair of hands.

"I will work tirelessly to bring football back to Fifa, and Fifa back to football," he said.

Ten years on, there can be no doubt the governing body is in rude health financially. It expects to report record revenues, external of $13bn (£9.6bn) for the three-year cycle through to the end of this year.

But those figures only tell part of the story.

They are boosted by the controversial Club World Cup, and the biggest-ever World Cup with its high ticket prices.

Last month, Infantino and Fifa were widely criticised for the proposal to sell stakes in its competitions - including the World Cup - to private investors, with football's global governing body ultimately scrapping the plan after four days of intense debate.

That led to Uefa declaring it had lost confidence in the Swiss, who has also clashed with players' unions and European football.

This is the story of his presidency and his legacy.

Uefa has 'lost confidence' in Fifa leadership

Infantino on the brink? Who might replace him if he goes?

It is easy to forget Blatter's successor as Fifa president was supposed to be Michel Platini.

But after Platini was drawn into the scandal at the organisation - both he and Blatter were later fully cleared of corruption charges - Infantino was thrust forward as Uefa's preferred candidate.

As the general secretary of European football's governing body, Infantino had been the right-hand man of president Platini for seven years.

But he was an unlikely saviour - a man who was rarely in the consciousness of the average football fan.

To many he was just the guy who presented Champions League draws.

Ten years on, you would be hard pressed to find a football fan who does not recognise him.

Turning Fifa around was no small task.

The US Department of Justice had indicted a large number of top executives and it needed root-and-branch reform.

Two pages of Infantino's manifesto were devoted to more than doubling development money for member associations.

That would be for new competitions, for infrastructure, and even to cover travel costs for smaller nations.

Expanding the World Cup was also included, though to 40 teams. Within a year it had been rubber-stamped as a 48-team tournament.

The election was a close-run thing.

In the first round of votes, Infantino led Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim al-Khalifa - president of the Asian confederation - by 88 votes to 85.

Infantino only moved clear when the 34 votes originally cast for Jordan's Prince Ali bin al-Hussein and French executive Jerome Champagne were reallocated.

The final score was 115 votes to 88.

"This is a new day, a new dawn," said then Football Association chairman Greg Dyke, welcoming Infantino's win. "He is not a politician and he is not an ego."

Infantino, meanwhile, declared he would "restore the image of Fifa".

"It's your money, not the money of the Fifa president," Infantino told delegates. "The money of Fifa has to be used to develop football."

Infantino was true to his word. But to make more money, Fifa had to be creative.

The controversial World Cups of 2018 in Russia and 2022 in Qatar were waiting in Infantino's in-tray.

In his early years as president, Infantino kept a fairly low profile. It was only when the World Cup rolled into Qatar that he started to become a more public figure.

Under pressure amid repeated criticisms about workers' rights and claims of modern slavery in the country, Infantino hit back.

He first called out "hypocrisy" and "racism" about Qatar in the European media, then made his infamous speech about discrimination.

"Today I feel Qatari," he said. "Today I feel Arabic. Today I feel African. Today I feel gay. Today I feel disabled. Today I feel like a migrant worker."

At every game he attended, TV cameras appeared to pick him out in the crowd.

And there was a reason. Reports, which Fifa declined to comment on, suggested television directors were advised that Infantino should be shown at least once each game, but not if he was on his phone., external

Fifa accused of breaching own rules with Trump award

Trump and Infantino - too close for comfort?

Fifa accused of creating 'fake' player unions

After the Qatar World Cup, Infantino made many more headlines - from hosting plans and new tournaments to disparaging remarks about the behaviour of England fans.

Infantino had promised an expanded, summer Club World Cup shortly after his election in 2016.

The plan hit several delays but - two days before the 2022 World Cup final - Fifa eventually announced it would go ahead in 2025, hosted by the United States.

It placed a large-scale tournament in a summer which was usually reserved for player recovery.

Fifa rejected claims players' union' Fifpro and the World Leagues' Association were not consulted.

Then came the unique allocation of the 2030 and 2034 World Cup finals.

It was decided the 2030 edition would be staged across three continents - Africa, Europe and South America. That meant the 2034 event had to go to Asia or Oceania.

With no realistic competition, it effectively guaranteed Saudi Arabia - another country with questions about its human rights record - would host.

Saudi Arabia and Fifa, under Infantino, had developed a close relationship.

Norway's football federation abstained from the process and argued the bidding process undermined "Fifa's reforms for good governance" and challenged "trust in Fifa".

In May 2024, it was revealed Infantino received a 33% pay rise, external - determined by an independent committee - upon his re-election the previous year.

It took his base salary from 1.95m Swiss francs (£1.7m) in 2022 to 2.6m Swiss francs (£2.3m).

On top of that, he was due a bonus of 1.65m Swiss francs (£1.5m), which was unchanged.

Infantino, who was earning about £1.3m when first elected in 2016, is now close to Blatter's final annual salary payment of £2.6m., external

However, a Fifa investigation showed that under Blatter leading executives were being paid huge bonuses running well into the millions., external

In November 2024, with the new-look Club World Cup drawing closer, Fifa unveiled the trophy - engraved with a personal tribute.

"Inspired by the Fifa president Gianni Infantino," it read.

Uefa was growing frustrated with Infantino's profile and his close relationship with US President Donald Trump.

It came to a head in May 2025. Infantino had been on a diplomatic tour of the Middle East with Trump and turned up two hours late for the Fifa Congress.

Uefa accused Infantino of prioritising "private political interests" and staged a walk-out.

Then came last summer's Club World Cup, which was characterised by stadiums with swathes of empty seats.

Yet when Infantino gathered the media at Trump Tower, he declared it to be "already the most successful club competition in the world".

In December, the draw for this summer's World Cup was a long, lavish and outlandish affair.

Infantino was front and centre, and Trump was awarded the controversial Fifa Peace Prize.

Within a week came the announcement of high ticket prices for the finals.

Group-stage tickets are up to three times the price of those for the 2022 World Cup, and the cheapest ticket for the final in New Jersey is £3,119.

After a minor climbdown, Infantino defended the prices and said they reflected the public's "absolutely crazy" demand.

Infantino insisted all the money would go back into the game, saying "without Fifa there would be no football in 150 countries".

He still had one more media mis-step to go before reaching his 10-year anniversary.

In February he had to apologise after saying it was "really special" no British nationals were arrested during the 2022 World Cup.

Infantino came to wider public attention, and attracted further criticism, during this summer's World Cup, which was staged in the USA, Mexico and Canada.

The tournament made headlines before a ball was kicked, with visas to the United States delayed - and even denied - for supporters, coaching staff and officials.

In May, Iran's base for the tournament was moved to Mexico after the US made it clear it did not want to host the team because of political tensions between the two nations.

That was followed by Somali referee Omar Artan, one of 52 officials appointed to work at the tournament, being refused entry when he arrived at Miami International Airport.

Fifa refused to intervene on Artan's behalf, saying it was "not involved in the host country's immigration process".

When the football did begin, Infantino's relationship with Trump was thrust into the spotlight when the US president asked Fifa to review Folarin Balogun's one-match suspension.

US forward Balogun was sent off during the last-32 tie against Bosnia-Herzegovina but was cleared to feature in the next round after an unprecedented intervention from Trump, which drew widespread criticism.

The fallout from the World Cup continued as Fifa opened disciplinary proceedings against Argentina over its behaviour after the final defeat by Spain and throughout the tournament.

The controversial plan to sell stakes in the organisation's major competitions prompted Uefa nations to agree to boycott all future Fifa competitions then led to one of Infantino's senior advisers resigning.

The plans would have allowed Fifa to create a commercial subsidiary to run its main events. External investors would then have been able to buy stakes in the company.

Fifa's chief operating officer Kevin Lamour said the governing body's own administration had been "deceived" about the project and UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham described Infantino as "the wrong man" to lead Fifa.

After a further two major confederations spoke out, Infantino released a statement saying it would no longer proceed with the plans, adding it had become clear the project had "created divisions" that are "no longer in the interest" of its original objective.

Uefa's response was damning - saying it had lost confidence in Infantino's leadership.

Despite the controversies, Infantino has made a clear difference to many football nations around the world. Yes, it is about money. But money for football.

He has enriched some of the poorest and smallest nations, proving funding through infrastructure and development.

And Fifa has been transparent in publishing the salaries of all top executives and keeping funds within football.

After being re-elected unopposed in 2019 and 2023, he is approaching another election year in 2027.

Infantino will be able to stand again, even though Fifa statutes limit the president to a maximum of three terms.

Only time will tell whether that comes to pass.

A version of this article was first published in February 2026
